readings.c1s1:
¶
'''bouse<sup>2</sup>''', '''bowse<sup>2</sup>''' (bous), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''boused'', ''bowsed'', ppr. ''bousing'', ''bowsing''. [Formerly also written ''bowss''; origin unknown.] ''Naut.'', to haul with tackle.

{{smaller block|After the rigging is ''bowsed'' well taut, the seizings and coverings [must] be replaced, which is a very nice piece of work.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 16.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To bouse up the jib''', figuratively, to get “tight” or drunk. [Slang.]}}

'''bouse<sup>3</sup>''' (bous or bös), ''n.'' [E. dial., formerly ''bous''; origin obscure.] In ''mining'', ore mixed with veinstone; second-class ore, which must undergo further preparation before going to the smelter. [North. Eng. lead-mining districts.]

'''bouse<sup>4</sup>''', ''n.'' Same as ''boose''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bouse-team''' (bous′tēm), ''n.'' In ''mining'', the place where bouse is deposited outside of the mine, ready to be dressed or prepared for the smelter. [North. Eng.]

'''boustrophedon''' (bö-strọ̄-fē′dọn), ''n.'' [< Gr. βουστροφηδόν, turning backward and forward like oxen in plowing, < βοῦς, ox, + στρέφειν, turn.] A method of writing shown in early Greek inscriptions, in which the lines run alternately from right to left and from left to right, as the furrows made in plowing a field, the plow passing alternately backward and forward.

{{smaller block|It has been noticed by Böckh and Franz that in the earliest examples of ''boustrophedon'' writing the first line is from right to left, and the second from left to right.
{{right|''Isaac Taylor'', The Alphabet, II. 34, note.}}}}

'''bousy''' (bö′zi), ''a.'' [< ''bouse''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''boozy''.] Same as ''boozy''.

'''Boveæ''' (bō′vē-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Bos'' (''Bov-'') + ''-eæ''.] A division of ''Bovidæ'', practically equivalent to the genus ''Bos'' in a large sense, or to the modern subfamily ''Bovinæ''.

'''Bovey coal.''' See ''coal''.

'''Bovichthyidæ''' (bō-vik-thī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Bovichthys'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of acanthopterygian fishes, typified by the genus ''Bovichthys'', having the lower pectoral rays unbranched and simply articulated, the ventral fins jugular and separated by a wide area, the anal fin moderate, and no scales. Only two or three species are known; they inhabit antarctic seas.

'''Bovichthys''' (bō-vik′this), ''n.'' [NL., < L. ''bos'' (''bov-'') (= Gr. βοῦς), ox, + Gr. ἰχθύς, fish.] The typical genus of the family ''Bovichthyidæ''.

'''boviculture''' (bō′vi-kul-t̮ūr), ''n.'' [< L. ''bos'' (''bov-''), ox, + ''cultura'', culture.] The breeding and rearing of cattle; stock-raising. [Rare.]

'''bovid''' (bō′vid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to the ''Bovidæ''; bovine.

'''II.''' ''n.'' One of the ''Bovidæ''.

'''Bovidæ''' (bō′vi-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Bos'' (''Bov-''), ox, + ''-idæ''.] A family of hollow-horned ruminants, the ox tribe, containing the bovines.
{{smaller block|The family was formerly nearly coextensive with the genus ''Bos'' in a large sense, including cattle as distinguished from goats, sheep, and antelopes. In this acceptation the family corresponds to the modern subfamily ''Bovinæ''. It has been found impossible, however, to draw any sharp dividing line between cattle and other hollow-horned}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bouse|644|bow}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''bouse<sup>2</sup>''', '''bowse<sup>2</sup>''' (bous), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''boused'', ''bowsed'', ppr. ''bousing'', ''bowsing''.   [Formerly also written ''bowss''; origin unknown.]   ''Naut.'', to haul with tackle.

{{smaller block|After the rigging is ''bowsed'' well taut, the seizings and coverings [must] be replaced, which is a very nice piece of work.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 16.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To bouse up the jib''', figuratively, to get “tight” or drunk. [Slang.]}}

'''bouse<sup>3</sup>''' (bous or bös), ''n.''   [E. dial., formerly ''bous''; origin obscure.]   In ''mining'', ore mixed with veinstone; second-class ore, which must undergo further preparation before going to the smelter. [North. Eng. lead-mining districts.]

'''bouse<sup>4</sup>''', ''n.'' Same as ''boose''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bouse-team''' (bous′tēm), ''n.'' In ''mining'', the place where bouse is deposited outside of the mine, ready to be dressed or prepared for the smelter. [North. Eng.]

'''boustrophedon''' (bö-strọ̄-fē′dọn), ''n.''   [< Gr. βουστροφηδόν, turning backward and forward like oxen in plowing, < βοῦς, ox, + στρέφειν, turn.]   A method of writing shown in early Greek inscriptions, in which the lines run alternately from right to left and from left to right, as the furrows made in plowing a field, the plow passing alternately backward and forward.

{{smaller block|It has been noticed by Böckh and Franz that in the earliest examples of ''boustrophedon'' writing the first line is from right to left, and the second from left to right.
{{right|''Isaac Taylor'', The Alphabet, II. 34, note.}}}}

'''bousy''' (bö′zi), ''a.''   [< ''bouse''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''boozy''.]   Same as ''boozy''.

'''bout'''<sup>1</sup> (bout), ''n.''   [A later and parallel spelling of ''bought''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   '''1.''' A turn, loop, coil, or knot, as in a rope or chain; a bend or flexure.
{{smaller block|<poem>And at the lowest end forget it not
To leave a ''bout'' or compass like an eye,
The link that holds your hook to hang upon.</poem>
{{right|''John Dennys'', in Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 150.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In notes, with many a winding ''bout''
Of linked sweetness long drawn out.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', L’Allegro, l. 139.}}}}
'''2.''' The part of a sling that contains the stone. —'''3.''' A going and returning, as in plowing, reaping, etc.; hence, as much of an action as is performed at one time; a single part of an action which is carried on at successive intervals.—'''4.''' A round at anything, as in some contest; a set-to; a trial: as, a ''bout'' at single-stick or fisticuffs.
{{smaller block|The gentleman will, for his honour’s sake, have one ''bout'' with you.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Look’ee, master, if you’d wanted a ''bout'' at boxing, quarter-staff, or short-staff, I should never be the man to bid you cry off.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, iv. 1.}}}}
'''5.''' A round of indulgence, as in drink: as, a drunken ''bout''.
{{smaller block|Here, replenish again; another ''bout''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iv. 1.}}}}
'''6.''' A turn or fit of illness: as, a severe ''bout'' of rheumatism.—'''7.''' In ''music'', an inward curve of a rib of an instrument of the violin kind, by which the waist is formed.—'''This''' (or '''that''') '''bout,''' {{smaller|this (or that) time or occasion.}}
{{smaller block|She got off for ''that bout''.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The Prince . . . has taken me in his train, so that I am in no danger of starving for ''this bout.''
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 1.}}}}

'''bout<sup>2</sup>†''', ''adv.'' and ''prep.''   [Early mod. E. and E. dial. var. of ''but''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   Same as ''but''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bout<sup>3</sup>''' (bout), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''   [Abbr. of ''about'', q. v.; now commonly written ''’bout.'']   About. [Colloq. or naut.]

'''boutade†''' (bö-täd′), ''n.''   [F., < ''bouter'', thrust, butt: see ''butt''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A sudden outburst or outbreak.
{{smaller block|His first ''boutade'' was to kick both their wives one morning out of doors, and his own too. {{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, iv.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''music'': (''a'') Especially, in the early eighteenth century, a composition having an impromptu and capricious character. (''b'') An impromptu dance.

'''boutant''' (bö-toṅ′), ''a.''   [F., ppr. of ''bouter'', thrust: see ''butt''<sup>1</sup>.]   See ''arc boutant'', under ''arc''<sup>1</sup>.

'''boute-feu†''' (böt-fė′), ''n.''   [F., a forked match-holder, formerly used for firing cannon, < ''bouter'', thrust, + ''feu'', fire, < L. ''focus'', a fireplace.]   An incendiary; one who incites to strife.
{{smaller block|Animated by a base fellow called John à Chamber, a very ''boutefeu'', who bore much sway among the vulgar, they entered into open rebellion. {{right|''Bacon'', Hist. Hen. VII.}}}}
{{smaller block|But the hardiness of Stuart’s opinions, his personal attacks, and the acrimony of his literary libels, presented a new feature in Scottish literature, of such ugliness and horror, that every honourable man soon averted his face from this ''boutefeu''. {{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Calam. of Auth., p. 202.}}}}

'''bouterolle†''', ''n.'' Same as ''boterol''.

'''bout-hammer†''', ''n.''   [For ''about-hammer'', equiv. to ''about-sledge'', q. v.]   A blacksmiths’ hammer; an about-sledge.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am for Vulcan now, for Mars no more;
If my wife scold, my ''bout-hammer'' shall roar.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'' (?), Faithful Friends, iv. 5.}}}}

'''boutisale†''', ''n.''   [An isolated instance; prop. ''booty-sale''.]   A sale of booty; a cheap sale, as a sale of booty commonly is.
{{smaller block|The great ''boutisale'' of colleges and chantries.
{{right|''Sir J. Hayward'', Edward VI., p. 88.}}}}

'''bouton''' (bö′ton), ''n.''   [F.]   Button.—'''Biskra bouton.''' {{smaller|Same as ''Aleppo button'' or ''ulcer'' (which see, under ''ulcer'').}}

'''boutonnière''' (bö-ton-iãr′), ''n.''   [F.]   A buttonhole bouquet.

'''bouts''', ''n.'' See ''boots''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bouts-rimés''' (bö′rē-mā′), ''n. pl.''   [F.: ''bouts'', pl. of ''bout'', end (see ''butt''<sup>2</sup>); ''rimés'', masc. pl. of ''rimé'', pp. of ''rimer'', rime, < ''rime'', n., rime: see ''rime''<sup>1</sup>.]   Riming words given out as the line-endings of a stanza, the other parts of the lines having to be supplied by the ingenuity of the person to whom the words are given.

'''Bouvardia''' (bö-vär′di-ä), ''n.''   [NL., named in honor of Dr. ''Bouvard'', director of the Jardin des Plantes, Paris.]   A genus of plants, natural order ''Rubiaceæ'', natives of Mexico and Central America. {{smaller|They are herbs or low shrubs with showy corymbs of red, yellow, or white flowers. Several species are found in greenhouses.}}

'''bouwery†''', ''n.'' Same as ''bowery''<sup>2</sup>.   ''Irving.''

'''bouza''' (bö′zä), ''n.'' Same as ''boza.''

'''bouze''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''booze.''

'''bouzy'''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'' See ''boozy.''

'''Bouzy'''<sup>2</sup> (bö′zi), ''n.'' A name given to certain sparkling wines from the small town and district of the same name in the department of Marne in France. The name is also given, inappropriately, to many other sparkling wines.

'''bovate''' (bō′vāt), ''n.''   [< ML. ''bovata'', < L. ''bos'' (''bov-''), ox: see ''Bos.'']   An allotment of land in early English village communities, the holder of which was bound to furnish one ox to the plow-team; an oxgang.
{{smaller block|The full husband-land, or virgate, was composed of two ''bovates'', or oxgangs, the ''bovate'' or oxgang being thus the eighth of the hide or carucate.
{{right|''Seebohm'', Eng. Vil. Com., p. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|Manifestly the ''bovate'' or oxgang represented the tillage, not of an ox-team, but of one ox of the team, that is, it was the share of the tilled land appropriated to the owner of one of the eight associated oxen contributed to the coöperative eight-ox plough.
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., II. 481.}}}}

'''Boveæ''' (bō′vē-ē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bos'' (''Bov-'') + ''-eæ''.]   A division of ''Bovidæ'', practically equivalent to the genus ''Bos'' in a large sense, or to the modern subfamily ''Bovinæ''.

'''Bovey coal.''' See ''coal''.

'''Bovichthyidæ''' (bō-vik-thī′i-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bovichthys'' + ''-idæ''.]   A family of acanthopterygian fishes, typified by the genus ''Bovichthys'', having the lower pectoral rays unbranched and simply articulated, the ventral fins jugular and separated by a wide area, the anal fin moderate, and no scales. Only two or three species are known; they inhabit antarctic seas.

'''Bovichthys''' (bō-vik′this), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''bos'' (''bov-'') (= Gr. βοῦς), ox, + Gr. ἰχθύς, fish.]   The typical genus of the family ''Bovichthyidæ''.

'''boviculture''' (bō′vi-kul-t̮ūr), ''n.''   [< L. ''bos'' (''bov-''), ox, + ''cultura'', culture.]   The breeding and rearing of cattle; stock-raising. [Rare.]

'''bovid''' (bō′vid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to the ''Bovidæ''; bovine.

'''II.''' ''n.'' One of the ''Bovidæ''.

'''Bovidæ''' (bō′vi-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bos'' (''Bov-''), ox, + ''-idæ''.]   A family of hollow-horned ruminants, the ox tribe, containing the bovines.
{{smaller block|The family was formerly nearly coextensive with the genus ''Bos'' in a large sense, including cattle as distinguished from goats, sheep, and antelopes. In this acceptation the family corresponds to the modern subfamily ''Bovinæ''. It has been found impossible, however, to draw any sharp dividing line between cattle and other hollow-horned ruminants, among some of which, as the antelopes, connecting links occur. Therefore, notwithstanding the familiar difference between an ox and a sheep, for example, or a goat and an antelope, the family ''Bovidæ'' now contains all of these which have hollow, persistent horns, common to both sexes, generally two, sometimes four, and certain common cranial characters by which they collectively differ from the saiga on the one hand and from the pronghorn on the other, these two so-called antelopes being made respectively the types of the families ''Saigidæ'' and ''Antilocapridæ''. The ''Bovidæ'' as thus defined are conventionally divided into five subfamilies: ''Bovinæ'', cattle; ''Ovibovinæ'', muskoxen; ''Ovinæ'', sheep; ''Caprinæ'', goats; and ''Antilopinæ'', antelopes. See these words.}}

'''boviform''' (bō′vi-fôrm), ''a.''   [< L. ''bos'' (''bov-''), ox, + ''forma'', form.]   Having the form of an ox; bovine in form and structure.

'''Bovill’s Act.''' See ''act''.

'''Bovinæ''' (bō-vī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bos'' (''Bov-'') + ''-inæ''. Cf. ''bovine''.]   The typical subfamily of the family ''Bovidæ''; cattle; oxen; bovines. {{smaller|They are of large size and more or less massive form. The head is carried low upon a short neck, the legs are relatively short, with the canon-bones little or no longer than the phalanges, the hoofs broad, the muffle naked, the horns simple and unbranched, and the tail tufted at the end. There are four inguinal teats. The leading genera are ''Bos'', ''Bubalus'', ''Anoa'', ''Bison'', and ''Poëphagus'', or oxen, buffaloes, bisons, and yaks.}}

'''bovine''' (bō′vin or -vīn), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [= F. ''bovine'' = Pr. ''bovin'', < LL. ''bovinus'', < L. ''bos'' (''bov-''), ox.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Pertaining or belonging to oxen, or specifically to the ''Bovinæ''; boviform. Hence—'''2.''' Ox-like; stolid; inert; dull.
{{smaller block|This ''bovine'' comfort in the sense alone.
{{right|''Lowell'', Three Mem. Poems.}}}}
'''II.''' ''n.'' One of the ''Bovinæ''.

'''Bovista''' (bō-vis′tä), ''n.''   [NL., < G. ''bofist'' (= Sw. ''bofist''), < ''bo-'' (of uncertain origin; cf. ''buffen'', ''puffen'' = E. ''puff'') + ''fist'' = E. ''fist''<sup>2</sup>, ''foist''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', in its orig. sense. Cf. ''Lycoperdon''.]   A genus of gasteromycetous fungi, or puffballs, closely {{img float|file=century v01 p0670 c3f1.png|width=120px|align=right|cap={{smaller|''Bovista ammophila.'' (From Le Maout and Decaisne’s “Traité général de Botanique.”)}}}} allied to ''Lycoperdon'', but differing from the latter in the absence of a sterile base, and in the structure of the covering or peridium, the outer part of which shells off. {{smaller|Three species are found in Great Britain and a number more in North America. Several species are edible.}}

'''bow'''<sup>1</sup> (bou), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bowe'', ''bough''; < ME. ''bowen'', ''buwen'', ''buȝen'', < AS. ''būgan'' (pret. ''beáh'', pl. ''bugon'', pp. ''bogen''), bend, bow, flee, strong verb, only intrans., = OS. *''būgan'' = MD. ''būghen'', D. ''buigen'' = MLG. ''būgen'' = OHG. ''biogan'', MHG. G. ''biegen'' = Icel. *''bjūga'' (preserved in pp. ''boginn'' and pret. 3d pers. pl. refl. ''bugusk''), bend; prob. = L. ''fugere'' = Gr. φεύγειν, flee, = Skt. √ ''bhuj'', bend. Orig. and prop. intrans.; whence the derived factitive form, AS. ''bȳgan'', ''biégan'', ''bēgan'', ME. ''buȝen'', etc., mod. E. dial. ''bay'', weak verb, trans., cause to bend: see ''bay''<sup>9</sup>. Cf. Icel. ''buga'' = Sw. ''buga'', weak verb, bow, make a bow. Hence ult. the secondary verbs ''bay''<sup>9</sup>, ''buck''<sup>2</sup>, ''buckle''<sup>1</sup>, and the nouns ''bow''<sup>2</sup>, ''bought''<sup>1</sup> = ''bout''<sup>1</sup> = ''bight'', ''bail''<sup>1</sup>, ''boul'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To become bent or crooked; assume a curved form; bend; curve. [Still in colloquial use in Scotland.]
{{smaller block|Better ''bow'' than break.{{right|''Proverb.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Like an ass whose back with ingots ''bows.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1.}}}}
'''2†.''' To tend; turn; incline.
{{smaller block|Thei ''bowiden'' awei fro the lawe of God.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Baruch iv. 12.}}}}
'''3.''' To bend or curve downward; take a bent posture or attitude; stoop.
{{smaller block|<poem>The flame o’ the taper
''Bows'' toward her, and would under-peep her lids.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|As to soft gales top-heavy pines ''bow'' low.
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, ii. 391.}}}}
'''4.''' To bend the neck under a yoke; submit or become subject; yield: as, to ''bow'' to the inevitable.
{{smaller block|On of us two mot ''bowe'' douteles.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 440.}}}}
{{smaller block|Often tyme it is betere to ''bow'' than to berst.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 34.}}}}
'''5.''' To bend the body or head in worship, or in token of reverence, respect, or submission: with ''to'' or ''before,'' and sometimes emphasized by ''down.''
{{smaller block|The rest of the people ''bowed down'' upon their knees.
{{right|Judges vii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|The evil ''bow before'' the good. {{right|Prov. xiv. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To ''bow'' and sue for grace
With suppliant knee.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 111.}}}}
'''6.''' To make a bow; incline the body or the head toward a person by way of salutation or friendly recognition, or in acknowledgment of some courtesy.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to bend; make curved or crooked; cause to assume and retain a bent shape.
{{smaller block|They rather breake him, than ''bowe'' him, rather marre him, then mend him.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 31.}}}}
'''2.''' To cause to stoop or become bent, as with old age or a burden; hence, to crush.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose heavy hand hath ''bow’d'' you to the grave.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Bow'' him, yet ''bow'' him more,
Dash that same glass of water in his face.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
